target_claim: Under the solution's own definition of a cut (any edge set whose removal disconnects G), the recursive decomposition procedure it describes outputs a partition of any cut E into disjoint minimal cuts (bonds); in particular it claims E\F restricted to component A is always a cut of G[A].
source_quote:
We will prove that any cut E in G can be expressed as a disjoint union of
minimal cuts.
test_sketch: Implement the described recursion: given cut E, strip edges one by one to find an inclusion-minimal cut F, remove F to get components A and B, partition E\F into EA/EB, recurse on G[A],EA and G[B],EB; assert at each step that EA (resp. EB) disconnects G[A] (line 0043's claim) and that the final output is a partition of E into bonds of G. Input family: small graphs (<=6 vertices) that are a 2-edge-connected core plus a bridge, with E = {bridge} union {one non-bridge core edge}. Concrete failing input: V={a,b,c,d}, edges {ab,bc,ca,ad}, E={ad,ab}. E is a cut (removal isolates d) under the stated definition, but F={ad}, A={a,b,c}, EA={ab}, and G[A]-{ab} (the triangle minus one edge) is still connected, so the asserted 'EA is a cut in G[A]' fails and no decomposition exists. Brute-force oracle: enumerate all set partitions of E and check whether any partition consists entirely of minimal cuts of G (minimality checked by testing all proper subsets for disconnection); the oracle returns 'no valid decomposition' on this 4-vertex, 4-edge instance, refuting the claim.
